newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil central bank says won't change forex policy.
newsitem.headline: Brazil central bank says won't change forex policy.

text.p: Brazil's Central Bank will not alter its foreign exchange rate policy under any circumstance and will use whatever monetary tools it deems necessary to defend that policy, a bank director said Tuesday.
Francisco "Chico" Lopes, Director of Monetary Policy, told Reuters Brazil's foreign reserves had recovered by July 15 to $59.5 billion, after slumping $1.7 billion in June.

"The Brazilian Central Bank will not under any circumstance change its foreign exchange rate policy," Lopes said in a telephone interview. "It (the policy) will be defended under any circumstance," he said, adding, "There is no possibility of that (a devaluation)".
Lopes also said he regarded today's sharp plunge in Brazilian stocks as a normal technical reaction following spectacular gains of almost 90 percent as of last week since the start of the year.
The Sao Paulo Stock Exchange plunged 6.54 percent this morning, while Brazil's C Brady bonds dropped 5/8 to 81.25.

The ripples from currency woes in Asia contributed to the turmoil in Brazil's financial markets, as some observers say Brazil also suffers from some of the same ills -- top-heavy public accounts and an overvalued currency.
Lopes dismissed comparisons between Brazil and Asian economies, which have become the target of currency speculators.
Thailand and the Philippines have been forced into de facto devaluations and the currencies of Indonesia and Malaysia have been pressured. The Polish zloty came under pressure Tuesday.

"We are in very different situations," Lopes said. "We are very calm and will maintain the posture we have assumed, no matter what circumstance," he said, referring to Brazil's forex and monetary policy.

Lopes said, "We consider that our priority objective is to combat inflation and we are not prepared to sacrifice the objective of battling inflation even if that means we have to have a tighter monetary policy."
"We are prepared to use whatever monetary policy we deem necessary (to defend our forex policy)," he said.
The Central Bank director said Brazil's foreign reserves had recovered to $59.5 billion by July 15 after dipping $1.7 billion in June.
"We are now with $59.5 billion today which means we are back at the best level of reserves we had this year," he said.
Lopes said that Brazil's external accounts were stabilizing.

"The worst of the trade balance is over," he said. "The current account has also tended to stabilize. We have a very strong privatization program and we see no problems in financing it (the current account gap)."
Brazil's current account deficit widened to 4.19 percent of gross domestic product in the 12 months to June after reaching 4.07 percent of GDP the previous month.
As for Brazilian stocks, Lopes joked that the bolsas had apparently been gripped by "an irrational exuberance" in early 1997.
"I think it's (the drop) a technical reaction, and the bolsa will recover," he said.
